step1_summary: Chief complaint: Progressive numbness and tingling of the left arm with subjective weakness.

Symptom details: • Began ~2 weeks ago after starting a boxing class. • Initially mild tingling, now constant numbness felt from elbow to hand. • Affects palmar aspect of 2nd, 3rd, and 4th fingers; occasionally shoulder discomfort with movement. • No significant neck pain. • Weakness interferes with piano playing; occasional object‐dropping. • Not relieved by massage, warm baths, or ibuprofen. • One episode of transient (≈20 min) loss of part of visual field in left eye a few weeks ago. • Occasional fatigue-type headaches; no seizures, no lower-limb symptoms.
Past medical history: Generally healthy; no chronic illnesses reported.
Medications/allergies: Ibuprofen PRN, vitamin D, occasional iron supplement, melatonin. No allergies noted.
Family history: Father – hypothyroidism, unspecified autoimmune disease. Mother – type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia. No known neurologic disorders.
Social history: 46-year-old right-handed female. Recently started boxing classes. Occasional alcohol binges; no data on smoking/drugs. Physically active.
Vital signs/exam: Tele-consultation – no recorded vitals. No formal neurologic exam findings documented.

V: Transient ischaemic attack / minor stroke: transient monocular visual loss + unilateral arm sensory deficit could reflect vascular event.
Subclavian/axillary artery thrombosis: arm numbness/weakness possible but less likely without ischaemic pain or colour change.
I: Multiple sclerosis: optic disturbance + focal sensory symptoms in a middle-aged woman; post-viral history.
Post-viral neuritis (e.g., brachial neuritis): arm sensory loss after recent flu-like illness.
N: Primary brain or spinal cord tumour: focal neuro deficits (vision, arm).
Peripheral nerve sheath tumour affecting brachial plexus.
D: Cervical spondylotic radiculopathy / disc herniation (C6–C7): dermatomal numbness after repetitive neck/shoulder activity.
Median nerve entrapment (carpal tunnel / pronator teres): classic 2–4 digit palmar symptoms.
Vitamin-B12 deficiency neuropathy: sensory changes, fatigue.
I2: Alcohol-induced neuropathy: episodic heavy drinking but duration short.
C: Thoracic outlet syndrome (possible cervical rib): arm numbness exacerbated by arm activity.
Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsy.
A: Systemic lupus erythematosus with neuro involvement.
T: Brachial plexus stretch/compression injury from boxing.
E: Diabetic neuropathy (patient not diabetic but family history).

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Cervical radiculopathy (likely C7 disc herniation/degenerative change)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Progressive sensory loss and weakness extending from elbow to hand in a dermatomal pattern; precipitating repetitive upper-body activity (boxing); shoulder discomfort; distribution (2–4 digits) compatible with C7 root involvement.
supporting_evidence: Numbness spreads from elbow into hand, not just distal hand.
Onset after starting strenuous boxing workouts (possible neck strain or disc injury).
opposing_evidence: No explicit neck pain or radicular neck movements described.
Transient visual episode not explained by cervical radiculopathy.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Median nerve entrapment (carpal tunnel syndrome or more proximal median neuropathy)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic tingling/numbness of palmar 2nd–4th digits; worsens with activity; repetitive wrist impact from boxing could cause or worsen CTS.
supporting_evidence: Palmar involvement of 2nd, 3rd and part of 4th fingers.
Nocturnal pain not asked but symptoms present at rest.
Repetitive hand trauma from boxing gloves/impact.
opposing_evidence: Proximal symptoms (elbow, arm) and subjective weakness of whole arm less typical for isolated CTS.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Female in 40s with separate neurologic events: transient unilateral visual deficit and evolving focal sensory deficit; recent viral illness could precede demyelinating relapse.
supporting_evidence: Episode of left‐eye visual field loss (possible optic neuritis).
Age and sex fit typical MS demographics.
opposing_evidence: Visual loss lasted only ~20 min (optic neuritis usually days–weeks).
Current arm symptoms confined to one limb; no dissemination in space/time yet proven.
No MRI or objective neuro signs documented.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Brief monocular vision loss followed by persistent unilateral arm sensory deficit could indicate separate or evolving vascular events.
opposing_evidence: Arm symptoms have persisted for 2 weeks (TIAs resolve within 24 h).
No vascular risk factors (young, non-smoker, normotensive).
No mention of facial droop, speech disturbance.
